title: Quentin and the House
premise: Sable Thornbury has spent years at Hollowmere Hospice perfecting the art of being unnoticed: counting doors, keeping lights on, and never acknowledging the backwards counting he hears from the dying. When an excavation crew unearths a door sealed from the inside beneath the hospice's oldest wing, the counting stops—and starts coming from the walls instead. Sable learns the house was built as a lid, and the song the dying hum is a lullaby keeping something below asleep; the harvest moon will rise on the one night the seal thins. In the climax, Sable descends and discovers the door was sealed from the inside by the hospice's first matron, who became the seal herself; to renew it, he must learn the song's last verse without singing along, holding the melody in his body while the thing below tries to harmonize. He succeeds at terrible cost—the house claims his memory of everyone he loves as payment—and the final chapter finds him a quiet, beloved nurse who keeps the lights on, counting doors, having traded belonging for the truth he can no longer speak.
about_author: Vesper Yarrow is a former night-shift caregiver who writes horror in the margins of old patient logs, insisting the best ghost stories are the ones that could be true. They live in a coastal town with too many locked buildings and one very old piano they refuse to have tuned.

chapters.title: The Arithmetic of Doors
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. We meet his rituals: lights on, doors counted, never answering the backwards counting he hears from dying patients. He is competent, invisible, and quietly lonely. When patient Edith counts down to zero and smiles at the ceiling, saying 'he'll want to meet you,' the emotional beat is dread wrapped in routine—Sable's invisibility has always felt like protection, and tonight it feels like being marked.

chapters.title: What the Excavation Wakes
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Crews digging the new wing's foundation unearth a door—iron-banded, sealed from the inside, warm to the touch. The foreman jokes; Sable doesn't. That night the hospice's counting resumes, but from below, ascending floor by floor. The beat is intrusion: the world Sable managed with rituals has a rule he never knew, and he's broken it by proximity alone.

chapters.title: Edith's Last Verse
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, with a flashback to Edith's final hours. Going through her effects, he finds a hymnal with a song missing its last verse, the page torn out, and a note: 'Don't learn it by singing it.' He interviews the oldest staff member, Marta, who goes pale and changes the subject. Beat: the first crack of mystery—the song is a lock, and Sable is already humming it without meaning to.

chapters.title: Marta's Silence
chapters.summary: Alternating Sable and Marta POVs. Marta's chapters reveal she was a young nurse in 1962, the year the last 'harvest admission' was sealed below, and that every nurse who learns the truth either flees or forgets. She warns Sable to request a transfer. He refuses—his loyalty is to his patients, who are counting for someone. Beat: loyalty vs. truth crystallizes; Sable chooses the patients over his own safety.

chapters.title: The Counting Ascends
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. The backwards counting reaches the third floor. Patients begin sleeping in perfect unison; a colleague, Dev, starts singing fragments in his sleep and wakes with dirt under his fingernails. Sable realizes the house is recruiting voices to complete the song. Beat: escalation and betrayal-adjacent fear—Sable must watch someone he cares about become an instrument.

chapters.title: The Matron's Ledger
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, deep in the hospice archives. He finds the 1890s ledger of the founding matron, Agnes Lowry, whose final entry describes sealing the door 'from the kindly side' and becoming 'the hinge.' The torn hymnal page is pressed in the ledger's spine. Beat: revelation—the last verse exists, but reading it aloud is the trap; it must be held, not sung.

chapters.title: Dev Sings at Midnight
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Dev, fully taken, gathers patients in the solarium to sing the song forward, and the walls count along. Sable breaks the circle by singing the melody wrong on purpose, buying a night, but Dev is found at the sealed door, fingertips worn bloody, smiling. Beat: the cost of loyalty—Sable saves the patients but loses Dev, and the harvest moon is two nights out.

chapters.title: Below the Kindly Side
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. On the eve of the harvest moon, Sable opens the door—it opens for him willingly—and descends into a mirrored inversion of the hospice where the 'admissions' of two centuries wait, patient and polite, humming. He finds Agnes Lowry, still the hinge, who offers him the truth: the house doesn't imprison the dead; it keeps them company so they don't leave. Beat: horror reframed as terrible compassion.

chapters.title: The Verse Without a Voice
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Climax. Under the rising harvest moon, the seal thins and the thing that is not the dead—the hunger the dead huddle away from—pushes upward, wearing Dev's voice and Edith's. Sable must hold the last verse silently in his body, mouthing it while every instinct screams to sing, while the house offers him belonging: a chorus, a family, a place where he'd never be invisible again. He holds the silence. The seal renews—with him as the new hinge.

chapters.title: Lights On, Doors Counted
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, months later. He is still the nurse everyone loves, though he can no longer recall his mother's face or why Dev's name makes his chest ache. The counting has stopped; the patients sleep in ordinary, ragged disarray. Marta visits, understands what he paid, and weeps for both of them. Final beat: belonging traded for truth kept—the last image is Sable, lights on, counting doors, humming a song he will never finish.
